pairs_out.input_result: Read together via n16->n17, the earlier chemistry/morphology-plus-overpotential result and the Coulombic efficiency (CE) cycling data show that the same two hosts distinguished by nitrogen-linked spectral shift, flatter/sparser vs dense-platelet zinc morphology, and a growing overpotential separation with current density (about -0.05 V at the lowest rate vs -0.10 V at the highest) are also the two hosts whose long-term cycling stability diverges sharply: CnC HS holds roughly 93-100% CE out to about 205 cycles, while C HS's data end near 50 cycles after falling to zero at about 40 and 48 cycles. The combination establishes that the structural/electrochemical distinction already tied to CnC HS vs C HS co-occurs with a large divergence in cycling durability between the same two materials, i.e. the host associated with the (comparatively) more favorable chemistry/morphology and overpotential behavior is also the host that survives far more cycles at stable CE.
input_limits: Does not establish that the overpotential separation (or the nitrogen chemistry, or the morphology) causes or predicts the CE cycling divergence; it only shows the two performance differences co-occur in the same sample pair.

Inherits the earlier result's unresolved confound: nitrogen chemical-environment change and flatter/more compact morphology still cannot be separated as the driver of anything, including the CE divergence, since they co-occur by construction in the same samples.

The two sides are different kinds of quantity: side A is a continuous, rate-dependent voltage difference measured at one time point across current densities (-0.05 V to -0.10 V), while side B is a cycle-count endurance/failure outcome (CE percentage tracked over cycle number, with C HS collapsing to zero at specific cycle counts). No dose-response or magnitude relation between the size of the overpotential gap and the size of the cycle-life difference can be drawn from mismatched quantity kinds.

Only two materials are compared, so this is a co-occurrence between two endpoints (CnC HS better on both axes, C HS worse on both), not a relationship established over multiple points or intermediate cases.

pairs_out.input_result: The same two materials that the earlier chemistry/morphology-vs-overpotential pairing distinguished (n14->n16: nitrogen-linked spectral shift plus flatter/sparser vs dense-platelet zinc morphology co-occurring with a plating overpotential gap that widens from about -0.05 V at low current density to about -0.10 V at high current density) are also the two materials that diverge in long-term symmetric-cycling stability: CnC HS stays within about 0.03 V out to 7100 min, while C HS develops growing voltage spikes starting around 2600 min and its trace ends near 4400 min at the noted battery-failure point. So the structural/chemical/electrochemical distinction already tied to CnC HS versus C HS also co-occurs with a large difference in how long each cell keeps cycling before instability/failure.
input_limits: Does not establish that the overpotential separation, the nitrogen chemical-state change, or the morphology difference causes the earlier voltage-spike onset and failure in C HS versus the stability of CnC HS -- it only shows the same two-sample comparison differs on both axes.

Because chemistry, morphology, and overpotential behavior all co-occur in the same two samples by construction, this pairing cannot say which one (or some other unmeasured host difference) drives the divergent cycling lifetime.

Mismatched quantity kinds: side A is a rate-dependent voltage-gap measured at two current-density points (a difference of differences), while side B is a cumulative time-course of voltage stability/failure over minutes of cycling; no dose-response or magnitude scaling between the two can be drawn.
Only two samples/traces are compared, so this supports an ordering (CnC HS more stable, C HS fails earlier) and not a quantitative relationship.
Inherits the earlier result's qualifications: the pyridinic/graphitic and Zn-N bond labels are the paper's interpretation, and neither the spectral shift nor the morphology was quantified.

pairs_out.input_result: Read together, the three-way co-occurrence already established (nitrogen-spectral shift, flatter/sparser morphology, and lower nucleation overpotential of 39 mV, all on CnC HS vs 43 mV on C HS) and the long-term cycling behavior (C HS voltage spikes growing from ~2600 min and failing near 4400 min, while CnC HS stays within ~0.03 V out to 7100 min) show that the same sample carrying the lower nucleation overpotential, the nitrogen-linked spectral shift, and the flatter morphology is also the sample that sustains stable, low-noise cycling far longer before failure. This extends the established co-occurrence to a fourth axis, in the same two-sample comparison: nucleation-overpotential ordering, nitrogen-chemistry difference, morphology difference, and cycling-life ordering all track together across CnC HS vs C HS.
input_limits: Does not show that the lower nucleation overpotential, the nitrogen-chemistry difference, or the flatter morphology causes the longer cycling life (or vice versa); it only adds a fourth co-occurring variable to the same two-sample comparison.
Does not rule out other structural, compositional, or textural differences between CnC HS and C HS as the actual driver of the cycling-life difference.
Only two samples/traces are compared, which supports an ordering (CnC HS outlasting C HS) but not a quantitative or dose-like relationship between overpotential magnitude and cycling life.

The two quantities being tracked are of different kinds: nucleation overpotential is a single early-cycle value (mV) while cycling stability is a cumulative, long-duration outcome (minutes to instability/failure), so their co-tracking is a pairing of orderings, not a measured functional relationship.

Inherits all qualifications of the earlier result: the pyridinic/graphitic chemical-state labels and any Zn-N bond remain interpretive, no coverage/amount/size is measured for morphology, and the overpotential values are read only at nucleation on the initial cycle, not across cycling or current density.

pairs_out.input_result: Placing the established PF/resistivity result (power factor peaks at x=0.01, ~29 uW cm-1 K-2 at 300 K, alongside the resistivity minimum at x=0.01) next to the ZT series (ZT at 300 K ~0.84 for x=0.005, ~0.78 for x=0.01, 0.63-0.69 for x=0.02-0.04, versus ~0.88 for the n-Bi2Te3 reference) shows that the composition where power factor and resistivity are optimized (x=0.01) is NOT the composition where the overall figure of merit is highest (x=0.005). The two optima are decoupled: the electronic-transport optimum sits one step higher in x than the ZT optimum. Together the two results establish that whatever non-n_H factor is boosting power factor and lowering resistivity at x=0.01 is not sufficient, by itself, to produce the best overall thermoelectric performance -- some additional composition-dependent quantity must be pulling the ZT optimum back down to x=0.005.
input_limits: The combination does not identify what pulls the ZT optimum to x=0.005 instead of x=0.01 -- ZT = PF*T/kappa in the usual decomposition, but no thermal conductivity value is cited here, so whether the shift is due to a lower kappa at x=0.005, a Seebeck-coefficient effect not captured by PF alone, or some other factor cannot be read off these two observations.

Both quantities are reported at 300 K here, so the comparison of optimum locations is only established at that one temperature; the earlier result's 623 K power-factor point is not matched by a corresponding 623 K ZT value in this pairing, so nothing here says whether the same x=0.005-vs-x=0.01 split holds at higher temperature.

The power-factor/resistivity optimum at x=0.01 was already qualified as not cleanly separating a resistivity effect from an independent Seebeck effect; that ambiguity is carried forward unresolved and layered under a further composite quantity (ZT) that adds thermal conductivity as an additional unmeasured ingredient.

The comparison is only of optimum locations (x=0.01 for PF/resistivity vs x=0.005 for ZT) across a handful of doping levels; it establishes an ordering/location mismatch, not a continuous relationship between power factor and ZT versus composition.

The DFT+Hall two-state, 0 K mechanistic account underlying the earlier result is not extended or tested by the ZT data; the ZT comparison sits on top of that unresolved mechanistic gap without closing it.
